name: French Contrast Circuit (squat, tuck jump, banded jump, banded swing)
setup: Four exercises done back to back as one round: partial-depth squat, vertical leap with a tuck, banded squat jump, banded kettlebell swing. Use a light squat load of about 50-55% of max.
execution: Do 4 reps of the squat, rest about 20 seconds so the potentiation is not lost, then 4 vertical leaps with a tuck, then 4 banded squat jumps, then 4 banded kettlebell swings. That is a 16-rep round. Rest 20 seconds between rounds and do 4 rounds (64 reps total, about 5 minutes).
cues: Squat sets of 4 at about 50-55% of max, nowhere near maximal, so you produce force instead of fatigue
Squat only to a depth that has something to do with your sport; no full squat
Take about 20 seconds before the jump; longer and you lose the potentiation
Move every rep as explosively as you can
Stay composed between rounds; do not rush the rest
errors: Going heavy or doing many squat reps, which turns it into a hypertrophy workout
Resting too long after the squat, which loses the potentiation
Finishing the round not tired, which means effort was too low
why: Coach John Meadows: an advanced session for a college or pro football player. The goal is to produce a lot of force quickly (rate of force development) and to keep doing it while tired, as an athlete must in a game.

defaultDose.reps: 4 squat + 4 tuck jumps + 4 banded jumps + 4 banded swings

contraindications: Needs adequate rest from other hard training

name: Banded Squat Jump
setup: Place the bands over the shoulders so they pull you down toward the floor; one band goes over each side.
execution: Jump up in the air against the band pull. The bands add resistance as you rise and force you to absorb a lot of force on the way down. Do 4 jumps per set, landing under control each time.
cues: Think "I am jumping out of a band"
Land well; the landing matters and loads the muscles eccentrically
The band teaches you to explode and follow through, because it gets harder toward the top
errors: Losing coordination and staying on the toes late in the round (fatigue; the band pulls you more)
why: Bands load the jump eccentrically and teach you to accelerate through the whole range.

name: Banded Kettlebell Swing
setup: Kettlebell swing with a band adding resistance (the bands are set so they pull the swing).
execution: Swing the kettlebell with light weight and generate as much force as you can on every rep. Do 4 reps as the last exercise of the round; the band makes the top harder, so follow through.
cues: Follow through; the band makes the top end more difficult
Arms back and drop down as fast as you can
why: The most accelerated exercise of the circuit; it trains force production while already fatigued.

name: Countermovement Jump Test (vertical jump monitoring)
equipment: jump mat or Vertec, or chalk and a wall
setup: Stand on a switch/jump mat, or beside a Vertec or wall. A wall works with chalk on the hand: touch the wall at standing reach, then jump and touch again.
execution: Jump as high as you can, however you like, from a standing position. Record jump height. Repeat under the same conditions each time so values can be compared over weeks.
cues: Same method and conditions every time
Chalk wall touch is crude but "better than nothing"
why: Jumps are among the best indicators of general athletic performance and are easy to repeat for monitoring.

name: Squat Jump Test
equipment: jump mat or Vertec, or chalk and a wall
setup: Get into a squat with knees at about 90 degrees, no countermovement.
execution: Hold the position, then jump straight up with a concentric-only push. Record height. It can be done weighted or unweighted.
why: Compared with the countermovement jump it isolates the concentric push from a standstill.

name: Short Sprint Test (5-10-20 m)
setup: Measure the distances with a tape. The video lists 5, 10, 20, 30 and at most about 40 m; most team-sport sprints are 20 m or less, so 30-40 m is often unnecessary.
execution: Run each distance from a standstill all-out and time it with a stopwatch (timing gates are more accurate but not required). Log the times.
cues: Keep distances to what your sport demands (0-20 m for field and court sports)
A stopwatch is "a pretty good idea of where they are currently at"
why: Sprints are one of the best indices of general athletic performance and need no special equipment.

name: Medicine Ball Toss Test
setup: Mark a start line and lay out a measuring tape.
execution: Toss the medicine ball as far as you can and measure the distance accurately. Repeat the same toss each time.
why: Cheap upper-body and trunk power monitor; only a ruler or tape is needed.

name: Repeated Sprint Ability Test (6 x 30 m)
setup: Mark 30 m. This is a power-endurance style test for team sports.
execution: Run 6 sprints of 30 m with incomplete rest between them. Compare the first sprint with each later one to see the speed and power drop-off.
cues: Record first-sprint speed and the drop-off for later sprints
why: Shows how well sprint power holds up under repeated efforts, relevant to court and field sports.
contraindications: Not a monitoring test to repeat often: it is very fatiguing
